You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.02 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.15 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.01 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 3 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

Design 1 'SECE_Diodes': failed the screen and was not tuned (topology 5b47f3b8a814).
S1 S pzp n1 ctrl=G1
D1 D n1 out DSCH
S2 S pzn n2 ctrl=G2
D2 D n2 out DSCH
G1 SYNC ton=0.001s phase=0 edges=pos
G2 SYNC ton=0.001s phase=0 edges=neg

DZ1 D 0 out DZ33
screen (out fixed at 1.8 V): S2: -1.81 uW of 21.6 uW needed (-8 %); S4: -1.81 uW of 3.24 uW needed (-56 %); S6: -1.81 uW of 9.82 uW needed (-18 %)
what this means:
- with the output fixed at 1.8 V, the net power delivered covers only -8 % of the load's need on S2 (heavy load), -56 % of the load's need on S4 (weak excitation), -18 % of the load's need on S6 (Cp +20 %, hot) (best of the value presets tried)

BEST DESIGNS SO FAR (values already tuned):

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $v_{out\_min} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$
        *   $v_{out\_max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (ripple)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.15\text{ s}$ (startup)
        *   $dv \le 0.01\text{ V}$ (settled)
    *   Piezo Model: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25 nF) and $R_{leak} = 20\text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   Operating conditions: S1-S6 (varying load $R_L$, excitation $I_p$, frequency $f$, $C_p$).
    *   Reference FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier): Failed ripple, startup, and $v_{out\_min}$ for S2, S4.

    *   `SSHI_FBR_Zener` (SSH: Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor) used a full bridge and an inductor-switch for voltage inversion.
    *   It passed the screen (power delivered > 100%), but the output voltage $v_{avg}$ was too low (e.g., 1.18 V for S1).
    *   Why was the voltage low? The full bridge diodes (DSCH) drop $\sim 0.25\text{ V}$ each. In a full bridge, the current passes through two diodes ($\sim 0.5\text{ V}$ total drop).
    *   The SSH inverter helps increase the voltage across $C_p$, but the bridge diodes are still consuming a significant portion of the available energy, especially at low excitation (S4).
    *   The reference FBR failed S2 and S4 on $v_{out\_min}$. SSHI_FBR_Zener improved power (screened ok), but still didn't reach 1.8 V in most cases.

    *   The goal is to raise $v_{out}$ above 1.8 V while keeping it below 3.6 V and reducing ripple.
    *   The full bridge is inefficient due to the double diode drop.
    *   An "Active Rectifier" or "Synchronous Rectifier" would be better, but we only have 2 SYNC controllers and 4 switches.
    *   Alternatively, we can use a half-bridge or a charge pump, but the piezo provides AC.
    *   A common high-efficiency piezo interface is the SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction) or a modified SSHI.
    *   Wait, the SSHI usually uses a switch and an inductor to invert the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks, then rectifies.
    *   Let's look at the SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction). It typically uses a switch and a diode to transfer charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$.

    *   **Option 1: SSHI with a more efficient rectifier (Half-Wave or Synchronous).**
        The SSHI in `SSHI_FBR_Zener` used a full bridge. Maybe a half-bridge or using switches for rectification? But we only have 2 SYNCs. If one is used for the inversion (SSH), only one is left for rectification.
    *   **Option 2: SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction).**
        SECE is known for higher efficiency.
        Basic SECE structure:
        - Piezo terminals $pzp, pzn$.
        - Switch $S_1$ between $pzp$ and $n_{mid}$.
        - Diode $D_1$ between $n_{mid}$ and $out$.
        - Switch $S_2$ between $pzn$ and $n_{mid}$.
        - Diode $D_2$ between $n_{mid}$ and $out$. (Wait, that's just a bridge).
        Actually, SECE usually involves a switch closing at the peak to connect $C_p$ to a rectifier.
        Let's try a simpler SECE:
        $S_1$ connects $pzp$ to $out$ (via a diode) at the positive peak.
        $S_2$ connects $pzn$ to $out$ (via a diode) at the negative peak.
        This is basically a synchronous bridge if the switches are the rectifiers. But we need diodes to prevent backflow from $C_{out}$ to $C_p$ when the switch is closed.
        $S_1$ (ctrl G1, pos peak) -> $D_1$ -> $out$.
        $S_2$ (ctrl G2, neg peak) -> $D_2$ -> $out$.
        Wait, this is just a switched-capacitor rectifier.

    *   **Option 3: Improving SSHI.**
        The `SSHI_FBR_Zener` used an inductor $L$ and a switch $S_1$ for inversion.
        $L$ was $0.01\text{ H}$, $S_1$ was `both` edges.
        The bridge diodes $D_1..D_4$ were still there.
        What if we replace the bridge with a more efficient arrangement?
        If we use SSHI, we flip $V_{Cp}$ at the peaks. This increases the voltage $V_{Cp}$ reaches.
        The bottleneck is $V_{out} = V_{Cp, peak} - 2V_{diode}$.
        If $V_{Cp, peak}$ is increased by SSHI, $V_{out}$ should rise.
        In `SSHI_FBR_Zener`, $V_{avg}$ was $1.18\text{ V}$. Let's check the piezo voltage. $I_p=50\text{ uA}, f=100\text{ Hz}, C_p=25\text{ nF}$. $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p) = 50\text{u} / (2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{n}) = 3.18\text{ V}$.
        With SSHI, $V_{Cp}$ can potentially reach $2 \cdot V_{oc}$ or more if the flipping is efficient.
        The issue in `SSHI_FBR_Zener` might be the $L$ value or the $t_{on}$.
        $t_{on}$ should be $\approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$. For $L=10\text{ mH}, C_p=25\text{ nF}$, $t_{on} = \pi \sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} = \pi \sqrt{25 \cdot 10^{-11}} = \pi \cdot 5 \cdot 10^{-5.5} \approx 3.14 \cdot 1.58\text{ uS} \approx 5\text{ uS}$.
        The tuned $t_{on}$ was $158\text{ uS}$. This is much longer than the optimal $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$. A $t_{on}$ that is too long will cause the voltage to flip back.

    *   **Option 4: Parallel SSHI / SECE variant.**
        Let's try a SECE structure that is known to be efficient:
        - Switch $S_1$ from $pzp$ to $n_{mid}$.
        - Diode $D_1$ from $n_{mid}$ to $out$.
        - Switch $S_2$ from $pzn$ to $n_{mid}$.
        - Diode $D_2$ from $n_{mid}$ to $out$. (Wait, this is still just a bridge).
        Correction: SECE typically uses a switch to connect the piezo to the storage cap only at the peaks.
        $pzp \to S_1 \to D_1 \to out$
        $pzn \to S_2 \to D_2 \to out$
        Wait, that's a synchronous rectifier. Let's try that.
        G1: edges=pos, phase=0 (closes at positive peak of $V_{pzp}$).
        G2: edges=neg, phase=0 (closes at negative peak of $V_{pzp}$, which is positive peak of $V_{pzn}$).
        This way, the only drop is one diode.
        $V_{out} \approx V_{Cp, peak} - V_{diode}$.
        Since $V_{oc} = 3.18\text{ V}$, $V_{out}$ should be around $3.18 - 0.25 = 2.93\text{ V}$, which is perfect!
        But we need to ensure it doesn't exceed 3.6 V. A Zener diode $DZ33$ on $out$ will handle that.

    *   **Let's refine the "Synchronous Rectifier" (Half-Wave x 2):**
        1. $S_1$ between $pzp$ and $n_1$.
        2. $D_1$ between $n_1$ and $out$.
        3. $S_2$ between $pzn$ and $n_2$.
        4. $D_2$ between $n_2$ and $out$.
        5. $G_1$ controls $S_1$: `edges="pos"`, `phase=0`, $t_{on}$ small.
        6. $G_2$ controls $S_2$: `edges="neg"`, `phase=0`, $t_{on}$ small.
        7. $C_{out}$ between $out$ and $0$.
        8. $DZ_1$ between $out$ and $0$ (Zener).
        9. $R_L$ is handled by the testbench.

    *   Wait, the piezo model is a current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$.
        $V_{pzp}$ will be a cosine.
        $I_{pzp} = C_p \frac{dV_{pzp}}{dt} + I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$.
        At the current zero crossing ($t=0, T/2$), the voltage $V_{pzp}$ is at its extremum.
        SYNC controllers close at the piezo voltage extrema (zero crossings of current).
        So $G_1$ (pos peak) will close when $V_{pzp}$ is maximum.
        $G_2$ (neg peak) will close when $V_{pzp}$ is minimum (so $V_{pzn}$ is maximum).
        This should work.

    *   Is this too simple? Let's check the power.
        In each half cycle, we extract the charge accumulated on $C_p$.
        The charge is $Q = C_p V_{peak}$.
        The energy delivered per cycle is roughly $2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} C_p (V_{peak}^2 - V_{out}^2)$.
        If $V_{peak} \approx 3.2\text{ V}$ and $V_{out} \approx 2\text{ V}$, $E_{cycle} \approx 25\text{n} \cdot (3.2^2 - 2^2) \approx 25\text{n} \cdot (10.24 - 4) \approx 156\text{ nJ}$.
        At $100\text{ Hz}$, $P \approx 15.6\text{ uW}$.
        S2 needs $V^2/R_L = 1.8^2 / 150\text{k} \approx 3.24 / 150\text{k} \approx 21.6\text{ uW}$.
        Hmm, 15.6 uW might be slightly low for S2 (21.6 uW).
        But the $V_{peak}$ will be higher than $V_{oc}$ because the capacitor $C_p$ is charging.
        Wait, the "Synchronous Rectifier" is essentially a switched-capacitor converter.
        The voltage $V_{peak}$ across $C_p$ will be $V_{oc} + V_{out}$ if it's perfectly timed? No.
        Actually, the current source $I_p$ charges $C_p$ for half a period.
        $\Delta Q = \int_0^{T/2} I_p \sin(2\pi f t) dt = I_p / (\pi f)$.
        $I_p = 50\text{ uA}, f = 100\text{ Hz} \implies \Delta Q = 50\text{u} / (314) \approx 159\text{ nC}$.
        Energy delivered per cycle $E \approx 2 \cdot \Delta Q \cdot V_{out} \approx 2 \cdot 159\text{n} \cdot 1.8 \approx 572\text{ nJ}$.
        $P = 100\text{ Hz} \cdot 572\text{ nJ} \approx 57\text{ uW}$.
        This is plenty for S2 (21.6 uW) and S4 (3.24 uW).

    *   One more thing: Startup time ($t_{up} \le 0.15\text{ s}$).
        $C_{out} = 1\text{ uF}$. $\Delta Q$ per cycle = $159\text{ nC}$.
        To reach 1.8 V: $Q_{total} = C_{out} \cdot 1.8 = 1\text{u} \cdot 1.8 = 1.8\text{ uC}$.
        Number of cycles $N = 1.8\text{uC} / 159\text{nC} \approx 11.3$ cycles.
        At $100\text{ Hz}$, $11.3$ cycles $\approx 0.113\text{ s}$.
        This is close to the $0.15\text{ s}$ limit. I should probably use a smaller $C_{out}$ to speed up startup, but larger $C_{out}$ reduces ripple.
        $v_{pp} \le 0.02\text{ V}$.
        $\Delta V = \Delta Q / C_{out} = 159\text{ nC} / 1\text{ uF} = 0.159\text{ V}$.
        This is way above $0.02\text{ V}$.
        To get $v_{pp} \le 0.02\text{ V}$, I need $C_{out} \ge 159\text{ nC} / 0.02\text{ V} = 7.95\text{ uF}$.
        But if $C_{out} = 8\text{ uF}$, $t_{up} = 8\text{u} \cdot 1.8 / 159\text{n} \approx 90$ cycles $\approx 0.9\text{ s}$, which is too slow ($> 0.15\text{ s}$).

    *   Wait, the ripple requirement is very strict ($20\text{ mV}$).
        $v_{pp} = \Delta V$ is the ripple from the switching.
        How to reduce ripple without increasing $t_{up}$?
        - Use a smaller $C_{out}$ and a regulator? (No regulators available).
        - Use a larger $C_{out}$ and... how to speed up startup?
        - Maybe the ripple is not just the switching?
        Wait, if I use a full bridge (FBR) as a base and add SSHI, I get the benefits of both.
        The FBR provides continuous charging (less ripple), and SSHI increases the voltage.
        But FBR has two diode drops.
        What if I use the "Synchronous Rectifier" but with a larger $C_{out}$ and I accept that $t_{up}$ might be a problem? No, $t_{up} \le 0.15\text{ s}$ is a hard limit.

    *   Let's re-calculate $t_{up}$ with $C_{out} = 2.2\text{ uF}$ (like reference).
        $t_{up} = (2.2\text{u} \cdot 1.8) / (100 \cdot 159\text{n}) \approx 3.96\text{u} / 15.9\text{u} \approx 0.25\text{ s}$. Still too slow.
        To get $t_{up} = 0.15\text{ s}$, $C_{out} \le (0.15 \cdot 100 \cdot 159\text{n}) / 1.8 \approx 1.33\text{ uF}$.
        With $C_{out} = 1.3\text{ uF}$, $v_{pp} = 159\text{n} / 1.3\text{u} \approx 0.12\text{ V}$.
        Still too high.

    *   Is there a way to get more charge per cycle?
        The SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction) technique actually extracts more charge because it doesn't depend on the voltage reaching a certain threshold; it just dumps the capacitor.
        Actually, the ripple $v_{pp} = \Delta V$ is the ripple on the storage capacitor.
        If we use a very large $C_{out}$ to kill ripple, we must use something to speed up startup.
        But we don't have a boost converter.
        Wait! The ripple $v_{pp}$ is measured in the *final window* (0.7-0.8 s).
        Is there any other way to reduce ripple?
        What if the current is delivered more continuously?
        A full bridge (FBR) delivers current in every half cycle, but the diodes are always on.
        The ripple in FBR is $\Delta V = (I_{avg} \cdot T) / (2 C_{out})$? No, it's more like $\Delta V = (I_{peak} \cdot t_{cond}) / C_{out}$.
        In the reference FBR, $v_{pp}$ was $26.2\text{ mV}$ for S1. That's very close to $20\text{ mV}$!
        Reference FBR results: S1 $v_{pp} = 26.2\text{ mV}$, S2 $v_{pp} = 20.3\text{ mV}$, S4 $v_{pp} = 20.8\text{ mV}$, S5 $v_{pp} = 43.5\text{ mV}$.
        The FBR ripple is much lower than the synchronous rectifier ripple.
        Why? Because in FBR, the piezo $C_p$ is connected to $C_{out}$ via diodes whenever $V_{pzp} > V_{out} + V_d$. This happens for a significant portion of the cycle, and the current is a smooth sine-like wave, not a sudden burst.

    *   So, FBR has low ripple but low $V_{out}$ (due to $2V_d$ drop) and slow startup.
        SSHI_FBR_Zener had $V_{out} = 1.18\text{ V}$ and $v_{pp} = 7\text{ mV}$ (very low!).
        But it failed $V_{out\_min}$ and $t_{up}$.
        The SSHI in `SSHI_FBR_Zener` used $L=10\text{ mH}$ and $t_{on}=158\text{ uS}$.
        As calculated, $t_{on}$ was way too long.
        If we use the correct $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p} \approx 5\text{ uS}$, the inversion will be much more efficient.
        This will increase $V_{Cp}$ at the peaks, which will increase $V_{out}$.
        Will it increase $V_{out}$ enough to reach 1.8 V?
